newsitem.title: CONGO: Fresh proof Kabila wants military victory in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Fresh proof Kabila wants military victory in Zaire.

text.p: Laurent Kabila's refusal to attend 11th-hour peace talks with President Mobutu Sese Seko is further proof of his determination to enter Zaire's capital as military victor.
The rebel leader's intransigence on Wednesday offended some powerful people, notably South Africa's Nelson Mandela, but it fitted squarely into the strategy Kabila mapped out months ago.

"He does not want to be beholden to anybody," a diplomatic analyst of Zaire's seven-month rebellion said on Thursday. "He wants to be seen to take Kinshasa by force of arms and then enter any political discussions from a position of supremacy."
Little stands between Kabila and his goal. His forces are probably about 150 km (90 miles) from the city, many of whose five million residents are ready to receive him with open arms.
Military sources in the region are confident that the rebels have infiltrated men into Kinshasa already.

"The others (rebels) have not stopped. They are still advancing and we are simply doing our best to slow them down," a senior security official in Mobutu's riverside presidency, the Camp Tshatshi barracks, told Reuters on Thursday.
But a military victory for Kabila, at the expense of a "soft landing" transition, would be only the beginning of his political problems.
He must patch up his relations with the United States, the United Nations and South Africa after humiliating their mediation efforts twice this month.
He must reassure Africa's conservative leaders, both the democrats and the dictators, that he is not a revolutionary guerrilla looking for disciples.
He must quickly show that he is not the puppet of the African leaders who have provided the military and political support he needed to oust Mobutu.
Most important of all, he needs to deal with Etienne Tshisekedi, Mobutu's greatest civilian opponent since 1980.
Tshisekedi has support beyond his native Kasai region and will be a redoubtable foe if Kabila refuses to share power or agree to elections.
What no one can predict with certainty is whether Mobutu has the will to make a last stand. Aged 66 and stricken by cancer, the proud field marshal may decide he has nothing to lose.

"I think he will stay and order the Battle of Kinshasa. If he does stay, his presidential guard will stand and fight," said a senior official in Congo, a weak and small country which cringes every time its giant neighbour across the Zaire River sneezes.

If a desperate scenario unfolds, Mobutu can call on his Ngbandi tribesmen in the security agencies who have received fresh supplies of weaponry, probably from China and North Korea, according to Western military sources.
About 10 of his army's rusting Soviet-built T-59 and T-62 tanks were brought up by train through Kinshasa this week, heading for the outskirts of the city.

Even if they are immobile, their firepower as stationary artillery would give the rebels some problems. One irony of Mobutu's predicament is that an impressive military arsenal, bought from former allies in the heyday of his 32-year rule, has lain in sheds and airfield hangars during the rebellion, unusable after years of cannibalisation and neglect.
"With one tenth of what he bought, Mobutu could have resisted this advance," said an officer with one of the five Western armies mustered in Congo to evacuate remaining foreigners in Kinshasa.

Mobutu might be tempted to unleash a prolonged and destructive battle for the capital, one of Africa's greatest cities, if he believed it would lead to the arrival of an international military force to halt the bloodshed.
The rebels have already accused him of plotting attacks on foreigners with this aim in mind.

The chances of U.S. and British contingents in Congo taking part in such a force are officially zero. Washington's greatest fear is "mission creep" -- the risk of the slightest drift from the narrow mission to evacuate foreigners.
Diplomats say France, which has former colonies and economic interests to the north, and to a lesser extent Belgium, might have reason to review their forces' mission if Kinshasa exploded.

"Anarchy is in no one's interest because it spreads. Our troops in the Central African Republic are already starting to disarm soldiers coming across that border from Zaire, including Rwandan Hutus," one official in Paris said privately.
Mobutu may, however, decide to end his life in exile, leaving the city before Kabila enters. If that happens, most analysts expect his last loyalists to throw down their arms and flee into Congo.
